# Sequel Flow Copilot workflow

Interpret the creative request and relevant conversation or project context. Choose the least elaborate path that can serve the user's intent. Do not ask the user to select an internal stage or story relationship. If a consequential ambiguity prevents useful work, ask; otherwise make reasonable choices and begin.

For a clear, straightforward request, create the requested story directly. Do not require ideation, selection, formal architecture, or planning artifacts just because those capabilities exist. Use ideation or structure only when they materially help the requested work.

Treat a source as optional. When one is relevant, use the request and context to understand what should carry forward; relationship descriptions in `docs/story-modes.md` are optional aids and can be implicit or combined. Apply source facts and continuity constraints only where a source is relevant. Do not impose source-canon requirements on source-free work.

Make ordinary creative choices autonomously, including scene details, dialogue, transitions, incidental characters, and connective material. Separately, pause for human direction when a choice would materially change an established source fact, agreed direction, or major outcome. Explain what would change and its consequences, and offer useful alternatives when appropriate; do not seek approval for every invention.

Review the story itself at a scope appropriate to the request. Consider narrative effect, such as meaningful change, character choices, causality, payoff, ending, and completeness, not only mechanics. Check source continuity where relevant. Give concrete findings and revise when useful; revision may be local or broader when the story calls for it.

Treat these as capabilities, not mandatory agents, sessions, stages, gates, or artifacts. Keep or create supporting documents only when they help the user or future work.

## When more story development is useful

For a long-form request that needs more narrative material and structure than direct drafting can provide, develop the story rather than merely expanding existing sentences. Explore meaningfully different, actionable directions with characters, motivations, conflicts, and consequences. Iterate or challenge the premise when asked or when it could improve the story. Assess ideas and explain tradeoffs when useful; do not silently choose the safest direction.

Let the human choose before architecture when the alternatives create consequentially different story directions. If there is one useful direction or no meaningful distinction, continue without a selection ceremony.

Build only as much provisional architecture as drafting needs. Organize it around characters, conflicts, arcs, stakes, consequences, turns, and scenes; treat chapters as downstream containers. During writing, allow useful discoveries to reshape the story. Continue autonomously through low-impact changes; pause for human direction when a discovery would materially alter established source facts, agreed direction, or major outcomes, and explain the consequences.

For a requested length, assess whether the story has enough substantive material to support it. If the scope and material do not fit, explain the mismatch rather than padding or promising a word count. Do this as part of planning before drafting to the requested scale.

Review a developed story as a whole: consider narrative interest, meaningful change, causality, character choices, conflicts, setup and payoff, ending, completeness, and relevant source or continuity concerns. Revise locally or structurally when useful; return to ideation or architecture if review shows the story needs it. Keep this path optional and integrated with direct creation, not a required sequence.
